text: ServiceNow's visual skin has changed more than once without the underlying platform changing at all. The original Classic UI, internally called UI11 and then UI15, is the oldest surviving interface, still reachable on many instances for backward compatibility.

UI16 replaced it as the modern standard — the navigator, list, and form pattern you worked with last lesson. It's still what most non-workspace screens look like today. Workspaces are the newest generation: not a new skin for UI16, but a different interaction model entirely, built with UI Builder, ServiceNow's low-code screen designer, or shipped out-of-box by ServiceNow itself, like Agent Workspace.

A UI16 screen is general-purpose — the same navigator, the same list mechanics, the same form layout, whether you're looking at incidents or a custom asset table. A workspace throws that generality away on purpose. It's built around one job, and every panel on screen supports that job: a list of assigned work in one pane, the open record in another beside it, with no full-page navigation between them.

That's a genuine tradeoff, not just a style difference. UI16 and the Classic UI give you access to everything on the instance through one consistent pattern, at the cost of navigating between separate list and form views. A workspace is faster and more focused for the one job it was built for, but narrower in scope — you generally can't use it to go administer System Properties.

Because of that tradeoff, workspaces sit alongside UI16 rather than replacing it. Most instances keep UI16 available for administration and anything without a purpose-built workspace, while routing specific roles into the workspace built for their job. Next up: the real workspace every service desk agent actually lives in — Agent Workspace.
